hints: Focus on what the ammonium ion, $\text{NH}_4^+$, can do when it meets a strong base like $\text{OH}^-$.
Notice the products are ammonia gas, $\text{NH}_3$, and water, which comes from $\text{NH}_4^+$ donating a proton to $\text{OH}^-$.
Check for the other types by asking if any solid forms, if any oxidation numbers change, or if heat alone causes the change.
walkthrough:
**Write what is actually reacting**

Think of solid ammonium sulfate as a source of $\text{NH}_4^+$ ions once it dissolves, and sodium hydroxide as a source of $\text{OH}^-$ ions. The key meeting is between those two ions.

$$ (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} $$

**Spot the proton transfer**

The ammonium ion donates a proton ($\text{H}^+$) to hydroxide to make ammonia and water. That proton donation to a base is the classic Bronsted-Lowry acid-base pattern.

$$ \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} $$

**Rule out the other reaction types**

No insoluble solid is made, so it is not precipitation. Oxidation numbers stay the same ($\text{N}$ stays -3, $\text{S}$ stays +6, $\text{O}$ stays -2, $\text{H}$ stays +1), so it is not redox. Heating just speeds up release of $\text{NH}_3$, the change needs the base, so it is not thermal decomposition alone.

options.A: Correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ acts as an acid by donating $\text{H}^+$ to the base $\text{OH}^-$, forming $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This is the standard test for ammonium ions.
options.B: Not precipitation. All the ionic products, $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{NH}_4^+$ salts, are soluble, and the observed products are ammonia gas and water. Students sometimes pick this because two solutions are mixed, but no insoluble solid forms.
options.C: Not redox. Check oxidation states: N is -3 in both $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{NH}_3$, and Na, S, O and H are unchanged. No electrons are transferred, only a proton.
options.D: Not thermal decomposition. The word heated is a distractor. Heat helps drive off $\text{NH}_3$ gas, but ammonium sulfate alone would not give this reaction, the sodium hydroxide reactant is essential, so it is a reaction between acid and base.
